## Boeing 2023 Form 10-K — Union Representation Percentages

Boeing's 2023 Form 10-K gives union representation figures in two places:

### Overall union representation (Item 1A, Risk Factors — p. 12)
> "Approximately **57,000 employees, which constitute 33%** of our total workforce, were union represented as of December 31, 2023 under collective bargaining agreements with varying durations and expiration dates."

- **33%** — the total share of Boeing's workforce represented by labor unions (≈57,000 of ~171,000 employees) as of December 31, 2023. Boeing also notes its union relationships span "10 U.S. labor organizations and 4 non-U.S. labor organizations."

### By union (Item 1, Business — "Human Capital," p. 5)
The filing's "Union — Percent of our Employees Represented" table gives the following:

| Union | Percent of Employees Represented | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) | **21%** | Two major agreements: IAM District 751 (Washington) expiring September 2024; IAM District 837 (Missouri) expiring July 2025 |
| Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA) | **10%** | Two major agreements: SPEEA Professional and SPEEA Technical, both expiring October 2026 |
| United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW) | **1%** | One major agreement with UAW District 1069 (Pennsylvania) expiring April 2027 |

So the three union-specific percentages are **21% (IAM)**, **10% (SPEEA)**, and **1% (UAW)**, which together make up the **33%** union-represented share of the workforce.

## Walmart Inc. fiscal 2022 Form 10‑K (year ended January 31, 2022) — pickup and delivery location counts

The filing gives these counts in Item 1, Business, in the segment "Omni-channel" discussions (as of January 31, 2022):

**Walmart U.S. segment** (page 7):
> "As of January 31, 2022, we had approximately **4,600 pickup locations** and **more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations**."

- Pickup: approximately 4,600 pickup locations
- Delivery: more than 3,500 **same-day** delivery locations
- Scope: the Walmart U.S. segment (Walmart and Walmart Neighborhood Market brands and walmart.com), covering pickup and delivery as part of its omni-channel offering (alongside ship-from-store and digital pharmacy fulfillment).

**Walmart International segment** (page 9):
> "As of January 31, 2022, Walmart International had approximately **2,900 pickup** and **over 1,900 delivery locations**."

- Pickup: approximately 2,900 pickup locations
- Delivery: over 1,900 delivery locations
- Scope: the Walmart International segment's 23 countries outside the U.S. (Canada, Chile, China, Africa, India, Mexico and Central America), covering pickup and delivery services in most of its markets, including same-day delivery in Mexico and China (via JD.com/JD Daojia partnerships).

**Important distinctions:** These are customer-facing pickup/delivery points only. They are separate from the physical infrastructure counts also given in the filing — 157 Walmart U.S. distribution facilities and 31 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers; 179 Walmart International distribution facilities, 83 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers, and more than 3,400 eCommerce sort centers and last-mile delivery facilities in India; and 28 Sam's Club dedicated distribution facilities. Likewise, the "more than 3,500 stores" figure cited for Walmart U.S. ship-from-store/direct delivery capability is a store count, not the delivery-location count. The Sam's Club segment (page 10) does not disclose pickup or delivery location counts; it only notes Curbside Pickup is available at all clubs and delivery-from-club is offered.

I retrieved Apple's FY2024 Form 10-K (AAPL_2024_10K.pdf, MD&A on pages 24–30 and segment note on pages 49–50) and traced the currency-related disclosures.

3. **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales** (up 4% to $30,658M from $29,615M): "The weakness in **foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar had a net unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024." (The increase itself was attributed primarily to higher Services net sales.)

4. **Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage** (up to $109,633M / 37.2% from $108,803M / 36.5%): "Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due to cost savings, partially offset by a different Products mix and the **weakness in foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar." ## NVIDIA Fiscal 2024 Form 10-K — Inventory and Excess Purchase Commitment Charges to Cost of Revenue

**Document:** NVDA_2024_10K.pdf (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024)

### The dollar amounts the filing gives for fiscal 2024

| Amount | Description | Where disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| **$2.2 billion** | Total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations charged to cost of revenue | MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (p. 40) |
| **$774 million** | Part of the above: the **inventory provision** recorded in cost of revenue (write-down of inventory to lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete inventory) | Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components, footnote (1) to the Inventories table (p. 68) |
| **~$1.4 billion** | Part of the above: the expense for **inventory purchase obligations in excess of current demand projections**, plus supplier charges and penalties related to cancellations and underutilization | Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components, footnote (1) to "Excess inventory purchase obligations" in Accrued and Other Current Liabilities (p. 70) |
| **$540 million** | **Provision release** resulting from sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations | MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (p. 40) |

### What each represents

- **$2.2 billion (total).** Per the MD&A: "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023." The two Note 10 components reconcile to this total: $774 million + ~$1.4 billion ≈ $2.2 billion.
- **$774 million (inventory write-down).** The write-down of on-hand inventory to lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete inventory — i.e., products/components in excess of quantities supported by demand assumptions. Per Note 1, once written down, inventory creates a new cost basis that is not subsequently written up.
- **~$1.4 billion (excess purchase obligations).** The accrual/expense for non-cancellable commitments to suppliers for quantities in excess of NVIDIA's current demand forecasts, plus related supplier charges and cancellation/underutilization penalties. This is the portion that relates to supply/capacity commitments rather than to inventory already on hand.
- **$540 million (release).** The offsetting credit, arising when previously written-down inventory is sold (releasing the new cost basis) or when previously accrued excess purchase commitments are settled/resolved at less than the accrued amount. It reduces the net charge to cost of revenue.

Arithmetic note: the filing does not state a single net dollar figure; netting the $2.2 billion of provisions against the $540 million release implies roughly $1.66 billion of net charges to fiscal 2024 cost of revenue, but NVIDIA itself expresses the net effect only as a percentage of gross margin, which is excluded per your request.

### Supporting context (no additional dollar amounts)

- **Note 1 (Inventories policy, p. 58)** states the mechanism: cost of sales is charged for inventory provisions to write down inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value or for obsolete/excess inventory, and for excess product purchase commitments; most provisions relate to excess quantities of products or components based on inventory levels and future product purchase commitments compared to assumptions about future demand and market conditions.
- **PwC's critical audit matter, "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments" (p. 49)** confirms this is the only critical audit matter, driven by management's judgment in developing provisions for excess/obsolete inventories and excess product purchase commitments, including assumptions about future demand and market conditions. (The $5.3 billion inventory balance and $16.1 billion of outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply and capacity obligations cited in that matter are year-end balances and are excluded per your request.)
- No separate fiscal 2024 dollar amount is disclosed for provision releases attributable solely to inventory sales versus solely to settlements of excess purchase obligations; the $540 million is presented as a combined figure.

**Sources:** MD&A Item 7, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (p. 40); Note 1 – Organization and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, "Inventories" (p. 58); Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components (pp. 68, 70); Note 13 – Commitments and Contingencies (p. 72); Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, Critical Audit Matters (p. 49).

## Boeing's 2025 Form 10-K — IAM District 837

The filing makes the strike and the current contract two separate disclosures, in two different parts of the document.

### 1. The 2025 strike (Item 1, "Human Capital" p.4; Item 1A Risk Factors p.11; MD&A Overview p.26)

| Item | What the filing says | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| Employee count | **Approximately 3,200 employees** | Employees represented by IAM District 837 at Boeing's **St. Louis area sites** (Missouri). Same figure used in MD&A. |
| Duration | **101 days** | Length of the 2025 work stoppage ("went out on strike for 101 days"). |
| Start date | **August 4, 2025** | Date the work stoppage was initiated ("the work stoppage initiated on August 4, 2025, which disrupted our St. Louis operations"). |
| End date | **November 13, 2025** | Date IAM 837 members **voted to ratify a new contract, thereby ending** the work stoppage. |

Impact described: disruption of St. Louis operations and impact on programs including **F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25 and Weapons**. Boeing also notes both the 2024 IAM 751 and 2025 IAM 837 strikes occurred **despite a tentative agreement with union leadership and leadership's recommendation that members ratify**.

### 2. The current collective bargaining agreement with District 837 (Item 1, "Human Capital" table, p.4)

| Item | What the filing says | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| Employee count | **IAM = 25% of total workforce** (of the ~182,000 total workforce; ~72,000 union members, 40% of workforce) | The IAM as a whole; District 837 is one of three IAM agreements listed. |
| Agreement | **IAM District 837** | Listed in the table of principal collective bargaining agreements. |
| Principal location | **Missouri** | St. Louis area sites. |
| Duration / expiration date | **July 2030** | The expiration date of Boeing's current IAM District 837 agreement. |

Notably, the filing does **not** state the term length (e.g., number of years) of the District 837 contract — only the July 2030 expiration date. (The Risk Factors section says generally that Boeing's agreements are "with varying durations and expiration dates," and separately flags two SPEEA contracts expiring in **October 2026** as a future risk.)

### 3. For contrast — the 2024 IAM District 751 strike (not District 837)
- Over **30,000** employees (Washington state manufacturing), strike initiated **September 13, 2024**, ended by ratification vote **November 4, 2024**, lasting **53 days**; halted production of most commercial aircraft plus certain BDS products (737, 767, 777, 777X; KC-46A, P-8A). Current District 751 agreement expires **September 2028**; District 70 (Kansas) expires **June 2027**.

**Key distinction:** the "101 days / ~3,200 employees / August 4 – November 13, 2025" figures describe the **length and workforce of the work stoppage**, whereas "Missouri / July 2030" describes the **terms and life of the successor collective bargaining agreement** that ended it (ratified November 13, 2025) and remains in effect as of the December 31, 2025 filing date.

All are fiscal 2025 / as-of-September 27, 2025 figures; I have excluded the prior-year comparatives (e.g., 38% for carriers in 2024, 44% for the largest vendor in 2024) and the 10%-or-more disclosure thresholds.

The filing states: "During 2025, the Company's net sales through its direct and indirect distribution channels accounted for 40% and 60%, respectively, of total net sales."

### Percentages relating to receivables (counterparties/groups of counterparties)

| % | What it measures | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **12%** | Share of **total trade receivables** attributable to **one customer** (a single customer that represented 10% or more of trade receivables) | Note 4, "Accounts Receivable — Trade Receivables" (10-K p. 39) |
| **34%** | Share of **total trade receivables** attributable to **third-party cellular network carriers** as a group | Note 4, "Accounts Receivable — Trade Receivables" (10-K p. 39) |

Gains on these sales are recorded as a **reduction of products cost of sales** when the finished products are sold, not as product net sales. (Risk factors, 10-K p. 16, add that these vendor non-trade receivables are "concentrated among a few individual vendors located primarily in Asia.")
- Also excluded: the "10% or more" thresholds themselves, which merely determine whether a counterparty must be separately disclosed; and Note 13's country-level net sales and long-lived assets (U.S., China, "other countries"), which are stated in dollars rather than as percentages, though the 10%-of-total threshold is used there.

## Pfizer 2021 Form 10‑K — Upjohn separation costs

The filing quantifies Upjohn separation costs in **two places**, and they measure different things: an expected total, and amounts already incurred.

### 1. Expected total separation costs — "approximately $700 million"

**Location:** Item 7 MD&A, "Overview of Our Performance…" → "Our Business and Strategy" (filing p. 26 / PDF p. 32)

> "We expect to incur costs of **approximately $700 million** in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, **approximately 75%** has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021. These charges include costs and expenses related to **separation of legal entities and transaction costs**."

**What it represents:** Pfizer's forward-looking estimate of the total cost of the Upjohn separation (the November 16, 2020 spin-off and combination with Mylan to form Viatris). The filing identifies the composition as separation-of-legal-entity costs plus transaction costs, and states that roughly three-quarters of the $700 million had already been incurred from inception through year-end 2021.

### 2. Separation-related costs actually incurred — "$434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019"

**Location:** Note 2B, "Divestitures" → "Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan" (filing p. 65 / PDF p. 71)

> "As a result of the separation of Upjohn, we incurred separation-related costs of **$434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019**, which are included in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*. These costs primarily relate to **professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities within finance, tax, legal and information system functions as well as investment banking fees**."

**What it represents:** The actual separation costs charged to the Upjohn discontinued-operations line — i.e., advisory/transaction and internal-separation spend rather than a forward estimate.

### Related figures disclosed elsewhere in the filing (distinct from the two above)

| Figure | What the filing says it represents | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **$52 million (2021), $44 million (2020), $185 million (2019)** | "Acquisition-related items" in the non-GAAP reconciliation, after tax; footnote states this "relates primarily to the **spin-off of our Upjohn Business**, and our sale of Meridian" | MD&A Non‑GAAP reconciliation (filing pp. 43–44) |
| **$585 million (2021), $2,879 million (2020), $6,056 million (2019)** | "Discontinued operations" adjustment (after tax) removing Upjohn/other discontinued results from Adjusted income | MD&A Non‑GAAP reconciliation |
| **$86 million (2021), $1,691 million (2020), $300 million (2019)** | "Business and legal entity alignment costs" in *Other (income)/deductions—net* — but these relate to the **2019 business structure change** (Consumer Healthcare JV), not Upjohn. 2020 also included **$292 million** in SI&A for "consulting, legal, tax and advisory services associated with a non-recurring internal reorganization of legal entities" | Note 4; MD&A non‑GAAP footnotes |
| **$2.2 billion** incurred Q4 2019–Dec 31, 2021; expected program costs of **$1.6 billion** (corporate enabling functions), **$1.1 billion** (commercial go‑to‑market), **$800 million** (manufacturing network optimization) | "Transforming to a More Focused Company" restructuring program — a cost‑reduction program triggered by the Upjohn spin‑off, but a separate program from the separation costs above | Note 3A |

**Bottom line:** the specific Upjohn separation costs are the **approximately $700 million** expected total (≈75% incurred through December 31, 2021), comprising separation-of-legal-entity and transaction costs, and the **$434 million (2020) / $83 million (2019)** of separation-related costs actually incurred and reported in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*, comprising professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities in finance, tax, legal and information systems, plus investment banking fees.

## Pfizer's Haleon Ownership Percentages in the 2024 Form 10-K

Pfizer's 2024 Form 10-K (filed February 27, 2025) discloses Pfizer's Haleon stake at four different points in time:

| Ownership | Point in time it applies | Where disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| **32%** | As of **December 31, 2023** | Note 2C — Equity-Method Investments (Form 10-K p. 66): "We owned 32% of Haleon as of December 31, 2023." |
| **Approximately 23%** | After the **March 2024** share sale — applied to dividends with a record date in Q1 2024 (recognized in Haleon's Q2 2024 financials) | Note 2C footnote to the carrying-value rollforward: "the impact of the reduction in Pfizer's ownership from approximately 32% to approximately 23% as applied to dividends with a record date in the first quarter of 2024, which were recognized in Haleon's second quarter 2024 financial statements." |
| **Approximately 15%** | As of **December 31, 2024** (i.e., after the October 2024 share sale) | Note 2C: "After the October 2024 share sale, we owned approximately 15% of the outstanding voting shares of Haleon as of December 31, 2024." Repeated in MD&A, Capital Allocation Framework—Haleon (p. 47). |
| **Approximately 7%** | In the **first quarter of 2025** (post-balance-sheet) | MD&A, Capital Allocation Framework—Haleon (p. 47): "In the first quarter of 2025, we sold an additional portion of our investment in Haleon for $3.0 billion further reducing our ownership interest to approximately 7%." |

### Supporting transaction detail
- **March 2024:** sold ~30% of the investment (791 million shares in a global public offering plus 102 million shares sold directly to Haleon) for **$3.5 billion** — this is what took the stake from ~32% to ~23%.
- **October 2024:** sold ~34% of the *remaining* investment (640 million shares in a global public offering plus 61 million shares directly to Haleon) for **$3.5 billion** — reducing the stake to ~15%.
- Total 2024 gains on these sales: **$945 million**; gross 2024 proceeds were $7.0 billion (per the cash flow discussion in MD&A).
- Accounting consequence: through Q3 2024 Pfizer used the **equity method**; after the October 2024 sale (loss of significant influence and board representation) it discontinued the equity method and began carrying the investment as an equity security at fair value, reclassified from Equity-method investments to Short-term investments ($5,411 million transferred; $217 million residual equity-method balance at year-end relates to other investments).

## Walmart FY2026 Form 10-K (WMT_2026_10K.pdf) — Receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency swaps

### Amounts as of January 31, 2026

| Amount | Figure | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| Notional amount | **$6,020 million** ($6.02 billion) | The total notional principal of the cross-currency swaps (Note 7, derivatives table) |
| Fair value | **$(920) million** — a liability of $920 million | The estimated amount Walmart would pay upon termination of the swap agreements as of the reporting date (Level 2, income approach, using interest rate and foreign currency forward curves) |
| Fair value, as stated in Item 7A | **$0.9 billion liability position** | The same fair value expressed in billions in the Foreign Currency Risk discussion: "The aggregate fair value of these swaps was in a liability position of $0.9 billion... as of January 31, 2026" |

### What the swaps are used for

**2. Critical Accounting Estimates (Item 7), p. 38**
NVIDIA explains that non-marketable equity securities "consist of investments in private companies without readily determinable fair values." They are measured at cost minus impairment, if any, and are adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for a similar investment in the same issuer (the "measurement alternative"), and "these adjustments may require use of unobservable inputs." - Gasoline and diesel demand recovered to pre-pandemic levels.
- Jet fuel demand remained below historical levels, reflecting continued COVID-19 impacts.

**5. Supply chain constraints**
Supply chain constraints, combined with the capacity reductions and continued demand recovery, drove a steady increase in oil and natural gas prices and refining margins across late 2021 and the first half of 2022.

## The increase: the 2022 acquisitions

Essentially all of the increase came from three business combinations completed in 2022, which added roughly **$8.45 billion** of new IPR&D to the balance sheet (Note 2A):

- **Arena Pharmaceuticals (March 11, 2022)** – provisional purchase price allocation included **$5.0 billion of IPR&D** (plus $460 million of indefinite‑lived licensing agreements and other, and $1.0 billion of goodwill). The principal IPR&D asset is **etrasimod**.
- **Global Blood Therapeutics (GBT, October 5, 2022)** – provisional allocation included **$3.0 billion of IPR&D** (plus $1.4 billion of developed technology rights and $1.1 billion of goodwill). The principal asset is **GBT601** for sickle cell disease.
- **Biohaven (October 3, 2022)** – provisional allocation included **$450 million of IPR&D**, chiefly **zavegepant** (the rest of the $12.1 billion of acquired intangibles, $11.6 billion, was developed technology rights for rimegepant/Nurtec ODT).

Together these acquisitions lifted IPR&D from $3.1 billion to roughly $11.5 billion before the impairment (the allocations were provisional/not yet finalized at year-end, so the components do not foot exactly to the reported $11,357 million).

The partial offset was a **$200 million impairment of an IPR&D asset**, disclosed in Note 4 (Other (Income)/Deductions—Net) and in the 2022 "Certain asset impairments" of $421 million. Pfizer's stated reason:

> "a $200 million associated with our Biopharma segment, representing an **IPR&D asset for the unapproved indication of symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy due to a mutation of the gene encoding the lamin A/C protein, acquired in our Array acquisition, and was a result of the Phase 3 trial reaching futility at a pre-planned interim analysis**."

The asset was written down to a fair value of **zero** at the date of impairment (fair value determined using the income approach / multi‑period excess earnings discounted cash flow method), with the charge recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net.

The other two 2022 intangible impairments (a $171 million developed technology rights charge and a $50 million PC1 licensing agreements charge, both from Hospira) related to competitive pressures and contract manufacturing forecasts respectively and did not affect IPR&D.

The significant IPR&D components at December 31, 2022 are **etrasimod, GBT601, talazoparib, Braftovi/Mektovi and zavegepant**. Berkshire's 2024 Form 10-K (BRK_2024_10K.pdf) gives three interlocking reasons for evaluating BHE on an after-tax basis, and it says so in two places.

**1. It is how the energy businesses are actually managed and evaluated.**
In the MD&A section "Berkshire Hathaway Energy" (page K-43), the filing states: *"The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."* Accordingly, the BHE discussion and the segment earnings table (U.S. utilities, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, corporate interest and other) are all presented on an after-tax "net earnings" basis, with percentage changes computed after tax.

**2. Income taxes are an integral part of how BHE's regulated businesses earn money — rates are set on a full cost basis that includes income taxes.**
The same MD&A page explains: *"The rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval. To the extent such costs are not allowed in the approved rates, operating results will be adversely affected."* So for a regulated utility, taxes are recovered through customer rates; tax items therefore flow directly into revenue and earnings rather than being a purely below-the-line item. Because a change in tax status or tax credit recognition changes what the utility may charge, pre-tax earnings would be a misleading measure of the economics.

**3. The magnitude of wind production tax credits makes pre-tax earnings meaningless for BHE.**
This is the explicit reason given in Note 26, "Business segment data" (page K-109): *"For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation."*

The numbers in the filing show why this matters. BHE's 2024 income tax line is a *benefit* of $1,871 million against pre-tax earnings of only $2,292 million, producing a negative effective tax rate of (81.6)%; in 2023 it was (215.1)% and in 2022 (51.8)%. The footnote to the table says the tax benefit *"Includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation."* Other disclosures reinforce this: the 2024 increase in U.S. utilities' net earnings included *"$157 million"* of income tax benefits from recognized wind production tax credits (page K-44), and consolidated U.S. income tax credits of $2,575 million in 2024 *"derive primarily from production tax credits associated with wind-energy generation of BHE"* (Note 20, page K-101). BHE also has meaningful non-U.S. tax items, such as the U.K. Energy Profits Levy and the Cove Point acquisition changing the effective rate at the natural gas pipelines.

**Consequence for the reader.** Because income taxes are considered at BHE in capital-allocation decisions, after-tax earnings are the metric that drives management's assessment of the business, so Berkshire's 10-K discusses BHE on that basis. This is in contrast to the manufacturing, service and retailing group, which is evaluated on pre-tax earnings (and pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues), and to insurance underwriting, which is evaluated on pre-tax underwriting earnings. ## The change

Net cash provided by operating activities was $12,744 million in 2024 versus $8,700 million in 2023 (2022: $29,267 million) — an increase of $4,044 million, which Pfizer describes in MD&A as a 46% increase.

## The causes Pfizer gives

**Primary driver: an increase in net income adjusted for non-cash items.** The cash flow statement shows net income before allocation to noncontrolling interests of $8,062 million in 2024 versus $2,158 million in 2023. Adjusted (non-GAAP) net income attributable to Pfizer common shareholders was $17,716 million versus $10,501 million, and adjusted diluted EPS was $3.11 versus $1.84. The MD&A attributes the higher pretax income from continuing operations ($8.0 billion versus $1.1 billion) to: a decrease in Cost of sales; higher revenues; and a decrease in Restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs. Specifically, total revenues rose 7% to $63.6 billion, driven by Paxlovid (including a $771 million favorable final adjustment to the prior-year $3.5 billion revenue reversal and $442 million of one-time deliveries to the U.S. Strategic National Stockpile), the addition of legacy Seagen revenues for a full year, growth in the Vyndaqel family and Eliquis, partly offset by Comirnaty declines and a $349 million unfavorable foreign-exchange effect. Cost of sales fell sharply because 2023 had carried $6,199 million of non-cash COVID-19 product inventory write-offs and related charges (including a $5.6 billion third-quarter 2023 charge of $4.7 billion for Paxlovid and $0.9 billion for Comirnaty) that did not recur in 2024.

**Offsetting factors.** Pfizer states the increase was "partially offset by the timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business," identifying two specific items:

1. **A decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid.** Deferred revenues for those two products fell from $5.1 billion at December 31, 2023 ($2.6 billion current, $2.5 billion noncurrent) to $2.2 billion at December 31, 2024 ($1.4 billion current, $785 million noncurrent), as amounts received in prior periods were recognized as product revenue upon delivery (including the $442 million U.S. SNS delivery), partially offset by new advance payments under amended contracts. Relatedly, the amount payable to BioNTech for the Comirnaty gross-profit split declined from $2.0 billion to $1.3 billion, and "Other liabilities" swung from a $595 million source in 2023 to a $3,115 million use in 2024.

2. **Net changes in inventory greater than one year** (see below). Related working-capital lines: Inventories used $854 million of cash in 2024 versus $1,169 million in 2023; Trade accounts payable used $1,023 million versus $300 million; Other tax accounts used $1,345 million versus $982 million; Trade accounts receivable used $109 million versus providing $347 million; while "Other assets" provided $3,380 million versus using $663 million in 2023.

## The cause for the change in inventories not expected to be sold within one year

Per Note 8A, inventories that are not expected to be sold within 12 months are classified as Other noncurrent assets (per the Note 1I accounting policy). These noncurrent inventories fell from **$4,568 million at December 31, 2023 to $2,663 million at December 31, 2024**, and Pfizer states the cause: **"The decrease from December 31, 2023 is primarily driven by a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, inclusive of the acquisition accounting fair value step up."** Pfizer adds that, based on its current estimates and assumptions, there are no recoverability issues for these amounts.

Supporting detail: In the finalized Seagen purchase price allocation (Note 2A), acquired inventories were recognized at $3,273 million as adjusted, "comprised of $1.1 billion current inventories and $2.1 billion noncurrent inventories" — the noncurrent portion reflecting the acquisition-date fair value step-up. That stepped-up noncurrent inventory was substantially drawn down and expensed through Cost of sales during 2024 as the Seagen product was sold, which is why cost of sales in 2024 continued to reflect the amortization of the fair value step-up of Seagen inventory.

For contrast, current inventories *increased* $662 million, from $10,189 million to $10,851 million, which Pfizer attributes to "higher inventory levels for certain products mainly due to changes in net market demand, network strategy and new product launches" (finished goods $3,775 million vs. $3,495 million; work-in-process $6,101 million vs. $5,688 million; raw materials and supplies $976 million vs. $1,007 million).

- **Purchase price allocation (preliminary):** $8,371 million of net assets, including $2,419 of property, plant and equipment, $1,438 of inventories, $9,997 of goodwill, $109 of acquired intangibles (primarily customer relationships, five-year weighted-average life), and $1,065 of off-market contract liabilities (expected revenue amortization of $113, $133, $129, $102 and $97 for 2026–2030). $53 million of acquisition-related costs were expensed in 2025.

Boeing excluded Spirit from its 2025 internal control over financial reporting assessment (to be done within one year of acquisition) and from Deloitte's ICFR audit scope.
- **Pension/OPB:** the acquisition added three frozen defined benefit plans and two postretirement medical plans to Boeing's postretirement disclosures.

### Bottom line

Per the 10-K, the acquisition's purpose and anticipated benefits are: **aligning Spirit's commercial production systems — including Safety and Quality Management Systems — and its workforce with Boeing's**; realizing **synergies (expected to be weighted to Commercial Airplanes)**, **safety and quality improvements** in the wake of the 737-9 door plug accident and FAA oversight of the 737 quality system, and the associated **production-system stability and rate-increase capacity**; and the resulting **strategic control of the Boeing-related commercial, defense and aftermarket businesses** Spirit supported. The filing frames these as *anticipated* rather than realized benefits, warning in its risk factors that integration difficulties could cause them to be achieved late or not at all.

**Only two of the six filings disclose a remaining transition tax amount as of fiscal 2021 year-end.**

**Total still to be paid: $32.9 billion** ($24.6B + $8.3B)

### Supporting detail

**Apple** — MD&A, "Liquidity and Capital Resources," under the heading *"Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable"* (p. 25 of the 10-K): "As of September 25, 2021, the balance of the deemed repatriation tax payable imposed by the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (the 'Act') was $24.6 billion, none of which is payable within 12 months." Apple lists it as a material cash requirement, and none falls due in the next twelve months, so the full $24.6B is the amount still outstanding.

**Pfizer** — MD&A, "Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements, Contractual, and Other Obligations" (p. 47): "Estimated future payments related to the TCJA repatriation tax liability that will occur after December 31, 2021 total $8.3 billion, of which an estimated $750 million is to be paid in the next twelve months and an estimated $7.6 billion is to be paid in periods thereafter." Note 5A (Tax Matters) corroborates the mechanics: an initial estimated $15 billion liability elected to be paid over eight years through 2026, with the third installment paid by April 15, 2021 and the fourth due April 18, 2022. The $8.3B total is the remaining amount (i.e., the $7.6B beyond twelve months plus the ~$750M due in 2022), not just the near-term piece.

### Why the other four do not state an amount

- **JPMorgan Chase** — Note 25 (Income Taxes) and the MD&A/notes contain no transition tax or deemed repatriation tax disclosure and no remaining-balance figure. Note 25's tax discussion covers only effective rate reconciliation, affordable housing credits, deferred taxes, and unrecognized tax benefits.
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — Note 19 (Income taxes) and MD&A "Financial Condition" disclose no transition tax amount. Note 19 addresses only indefinite reinvestment, tax expense by jurisdiction, effective rate reconciliation, and unrecognized tax benefits.
- **ExxonMobil** — Note 19 (Income and Other Taxes) and the MD&A "Taxes" and "Contractual Obligations" sections disclose no transition tax amount. Note 19 covers tax expense, effective rate reconciliation, deferred taxes, and unrecognized tax benefits only; the contractual obligations table lists take-or-pay and purchase obligations, with no transition tax line.
- **Boeing** — Note 4 (Income Taxes) mentions the TCJA only to note that "The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) one-time repatriation tax and Global Intangible Low Tax Income liabilities effectively taxed the undistributed earnings previously deferred from U.S. income taxes," with no amount. Boeing's "Capital Resources" contractual obligations table lists long-term debt, interest, pension/postretirement, purchase obligations, and 737 MAX customer concessions — no transition tax line. Accrued liabilities (Note 13) show income taxes payable of only $5 million.

**One caveat on the two disclosed figures:** both are rounded to the nearest $100 million, and each company notes the obligation can change (e.g., Pfizer: "Our obligations may vary as a result of changes in our uncertain tax positions and/or availability of attributes such as foreign tax and other credit carryforwards"). So $32.9 billion is the sum of the two disclosed amounts rather than a figure any of the filings itself presents.
